title: Garnets in the mud
teaches: How heat and pressure alter buried rock in the solid state, and how the resulting minerals record the depth of burial

blocks.text: A nearly straight geological boundary divides Scotland in two. South of it lies the Midland Valley, low country of red sandstone and farmland; north of it rise the Highlands. The dividing line is the **Highland Boundary Fault**, a fracture in the crust along which the rock on one side has shifted against the rock on the other, running across the country from the Isle of Arran in the southwest to Stonehaven on the North Sea coast.

blocks.caption: The southeastern Highlands. The red line marks the Highland Boundary Fault; north of it, Glen Esk and Glen Clova cut up into the hills.

options.title: The Highland edge
options.alt: A shaded relief map of the southeastern Scottish Highlands, with the Highland Boundary Fault running from southwest to northeast between lowland and hills, and Glen Esk, Glen Clova, Edzell, Kirriemuir and Stonehaven marked.

blocks.text: If you cross the fault near Edzell and walk north up Glen Esk, the rocks change under your feet. At first they are grey slates, the kind once split for roofs. A few miles on they take on a silky sheen. Farther still, they glitter in the light, studded with pea-sized, dark-red crystals of **garnet**. Higher up the glen come brown crystals of staurolite, then blue blades of kyanite, and at last a coarse rock striped in pale and dark bands.

blocks.caption: Garnet schist: dark red garnets set in a glittering matrix of mica flakes.

blocks.text: Yet all of these rocks began as the same material. Near the fault, where the alteration is slightest, the original beds of sand and mud are still intact, and in places even preserve ripple marks like those in lesson 2. Farther north those sedimentary features fade, but individual beds can be traced on foot from one mineral zone into the next. Before they grew garnets and kyanite, the rocks of Glen Esk were ordinary marine muds and sands, no different from the sediment that hardens into shale.

blocks.caption: Shale: compacted, fine-grained mud that splits along its original bedding planes.

blocks.text: Some process took ordinary marine mud and recrystallised it into a rock full of garnets, and did so with increasing intensity the farther north one walks into the hills.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: North of the Highland Boundary Fault, rocks that began as marine mud and sand grade from slate into garnet-bearing schist and banded gneiss.
The degree of alteration increases steadily northward into the Highlands.

blocks.text: A rock buried deep in the crust is subjected to both heat and pressure. The heat comes from the Earth's interior, which is kept warm in large part by the slow decay of radioactive elements in the crust and mantle; in most continental crust, measured in deep mines and boreholes, temperature rises by about 25 °C for every kilometre of depth. The pressure comes both from the dead weight of the overlying rock and from horizontal compression. The Earth's outer shell is divided into rigid **plates** that move at a few centimetres a year, and where two plates converge, the crust between them crumples and thickens into a mountain belt, forcing surface rocks tens of kilometres down.

Heat and pressure can remake a rock without melting it. While the rock remains completely solid, atoms migrate through the crystal lattices and recombine into new minerals that are stable under the higher temperatures and pressures. A rock altered in the solid state in this way is **metamorphic**, from the Greek for change of form.

Directed pressure also reorganises the rock's texture. Mud consists mostly of microscopic, flat clay platelets oriented at random. When the mud is compressed from one direction, existing flakes rotate and new sheets of **mica** and related platy minerals crystallise perpendicular to the squeeze, aligning themselves like pages pressed flat under a heavy book.

blocks.caption: A close-up of mud under compression and heat. The pale streaks represent microscopic flakes of clay and mica.
blocks.task: Compress the rock until it develops a splitting plane along the aligned flakes

blocks.text: Once the platy minerals share a common alignment, the rock splits readily along them, much as a deck of cards parts between cards. This plane of splitting, called **cleavage** or **foliation**, commonly cuts straight across the original sedimentary bedding, which may survive only as faint colour bands on a split face. In **slate**, the aligned flakes are still too small to see with the naked eye, allowing the rock to be cleaved into thin, smooth roofing tiles. At higher temperatures, atoms diffuse more rapidly and the crystals grow larger: the rock becomes first a silky **phyllite**, and then a **schist**, in which individual mica flakes are large enough to catch the light on every surface.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Deep burial subjects rock to rising temperature and directed pressure.
Metamorphism is the solid-state recrystallisation of a rock into new minerals stable at higher temperatures and pressures.
Platy minerals grow perpendicular to compression, giving slate, phyllite and schist their planar splitting.

blocks.text: In the 1880s and 1890s, George Barrow of the Geological Survey walked these glens outcrop by outcrop to map the country rock. He realised that the metamorphic minerals in the former mudstones appear in a strict order rather than at random. As one walks north from the Highland Boundary Fault, each new mineral makes its first appearance along a distinct boundary line on the map, and remains present across the ground beyond it. These boundaries run roughly parallel to the fault, dividing the countryside into progressive bands. Barrow named each band, or **zone**, after the **index mineral** that first appears within it.

Heading north up the glens, Barrow's zones are marked in turn by **chlorite**, a greenish platy mineral; **biotite**, a dark mica; red **garnet**; brown crystals of **staurolite**; blue blades of **kyanite**; and fine white needles of **sillimanite**. The sequence in Glen Esk matched the sequence in Glen Clova, and geologists subsequently recognised the same progression of index minerals in worn-down mountain belts around the world, including the Alps and the Appalachians.

blocks.caption: Mica schist containing red garnets and brown staurolite crystals, with aligned mica flakes catching the light.

blocks.text: Because each index mineral is stable only within a specific window of temperature and pressure, the mineral assemblage left in a rock records the conditions it reached at its deepest burial. The chart below plots temperature horizontally and depth vertically, with the dashed line tracing the **geothermal gradient**, the rate at which temperature climbs with depth.

blocks.caption: Temperature across, depth down. The dashed line is the geothermal gradient; the dot tracks the buried rock.
blocks.task: Adjust the depth until the rock enters the garnet stability field

blocks.text: Under a typical continental gradient of about 25 °C per kilometre, mudstone enters the garnet zone at a depth of roughly 20 km. Kyanite requires both higher temperatures and substantial pressure; if a rock is heated to the same degree at depths shallower than about 14 km, for instance right beside a hot granite intrusion, the same atoms arrange themselves into a lower-pressure mineral called **andalusite** instead. Conversely, where one tectonic plate dives rapidly beneath another, dragging cold crust to great depth before it can warm up (a gradient below about 10 °C per kilometre), the rock recrystallises into a dense, bluish rock called **blueschist**. Above roughly 700 °C, the rock begins to melt.

blocks.caption: Blue blades of kyanite, an aluminium silicate mineral that forms only at high pressures deep in the crust.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Barrow's index minerals (chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite) appear in a predictable sequence of increasing metamorphic grade.
Because each mineral is stable over a limited range of temperature and pressure, a rock's mineral assemblage records the depth and heat it experienced.

parts.title: The roots of a mountain range

blocks.text: Barrow himself attributed the heat to buried granite intrusions, and local magmatic heating did play a part, especially at the highest temperatures. The broader pattern, however, reflects regional burial during a collision. Around 470 million years ago, during the Grampian phase of the Caledonian mountain-building event, a chain of volcanic islands collided with the margin of the ancient continent that included Scotland. (That date comes from the radioactive decay of elements locked inside the crystals, a subject for a later lesson.) The continental margin crumpled and thickened into a mountain belt on the scale of the modern Himalaya, forcing the marine muds and sands in its core 20 kilometres or more into the crust, where they grew garnets and kyanite.

Over the tens of millions of years that followed, the mountains were stripped away by weather and rivers. Because the relatively light continental crust floats on the denser, slowly deforming mantle beneath it, much like a loaded barge in water, unloading the top of the range caused the deep crust to rebound upward. For kyanite-bearing schists formed at a depth of 25 kilometres to sit at the modern surface, roughly 25 kilometres of overlying rock had to be eroded from above them. A walk up Glen Esk today is a walk across the exhumed roots of that range, ending in the banded **gneiss** where the deepest rocks came close to melting.

blocks.caption: Gneiss: at temperatures approaching melting, light and dark minerals segregate into coarse bands.

blocks.text: Just across the Highland Boundary Fault, the red sandstones of the Midland Valley tell the other half of the story. Those sandstones were never deeply buried, and they contain rounded pebbles of Highland schist and vein quartz washed out of the rising mountains by ancient rivers, proving that the sandstones are younger than the metamorphism of the rocks that supplied their gravel. Surface-formed sediments now lie directly alongside rocks that crystallised 20 kilometres or more underground. The time required to raise and then erase a mountain range of that scale, and how geologists first worked out the span of time involved, is the subject of the next lessons.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The Scottish Highlands are the deeply eroded core of a Caledonian mountain range formed about 470 million years ago.
As erosion stripped the upper kilometres of the range, buoyant rebound lifted the deep metamorphic roots to the surface.
High-grade metamorphic minerals at the surface indicate how much overlying crust has been removed.

blocks.caption: Six questions on metamorphic rocks
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: This schist is studded with red garnets and shiny flakes of mica. What was the rock before it was metamorphosed?
choices: Marine mud or shale laid down in water
items.why: The garnets and mica grew in the solid state as the rock was heated and compressed; near the Highland Boundary Fault, the same beds still preserve their original sedimentary layering.

items.ask: How does a rock acquire a new set of minerals during metamorphism?
choices: Its atoms diffuse and rearrange into new crystal structures while the rock remains solid
The rock melts completely and crystallises new minerals as it cools
Groundwater dissolves the original rock and precipitates new minerals in the void
items.why: Metamorphism takes place in the solid state. Once a rock melts completely, any rock that crystallises from the melt is classified as igneous.

items.ask: Why does roofing slate split so cleanly into thin, flat sheets?
choices: Microscopic mica and clay flakes have grown or rotated to lie parallel to one another, perpendicular to the direction of compression
It splits along the original layers of mud laid down on the sea floor
It developed parallel cooling cracks as it solidified
items.why: Directed pressure aligns the platy minerals into a pervasive cleavage that often cuts right across the original sedimentary bedding.

items.ask: Walking north up Glen Esk, you pass from garnet schist into kyanite schist. What does this transition indicate?
choices: The rocks farther north reached higher temperatures and pressures at greater depth
The rocks farther north cooled more slowly from a magma chamber
The original muds farther north were deposited much earlier
items.why: Kyanite requires higher temperatures and pressures than garnet to crystallise, recording deeper burial in the thickened mountain root.

items.ask: A slab of crust is carried 30 km down in a subduction zone, warming at only 8 °C per kilometre. What rock does it form?
items.why: High pressure combined with low temperature produces blueschist, characteristic of cold crust dragged rapidly down a subduction zone. Under a normal 25 °C/km gradient, 30 km of burial would produce high-grade gneiss or partial melting.

items.ask: If kyanite and garnet crystallise 20 to 25 km underground, how did these Highland rocks reach the modern surface?
choices: Erosion stripped away the overlying mountain range, and the unloaded crust rose buoyantly in response
The hot schists were buoyant enough to punch their way up through 20 km of solid rock
The surrounding lowlands subsided by 20 km, leaving the deep rocks exposed
items.why: As weather and rivers removed kilometres of rock from the top of the range, buoyant rebound of the crust lifted the deep root upward until it was exposed at the surface.

summary: **Buried rock changes without melting.** Heat and pressure recrystallise it into metamorphic rock.
**Squeezing lines up the minerals.** Platy minerals like mica grow aligned, giving slate, phyllite and schist their layered splitting.
**Index minerals record depth and heat.** From chlorite through biotite, garnet and kyanite to sillimanite, each marks a higher grade of temperature and pressure.
**A map of index minerals is a map of conditions.** Zones across a region show how deeply each part was buried and heated.
**Old mountains leave their roots exposed.** The Scottish Highlands are the worn-down metamorphic core of an ancient mountain belt.
